claim: More than a quarter of drugs fail clinical trials due to lack of efficacy.

claim: The study analyzed in vitro screening data on 265 compounds across 1074 cancer cell lines.
source: Applied to in vitro screening data on 265 compounds across 1074 cancer cell lines, our models identified 24 clinically established drug-response biomarkers

claim: The GP models identified 24 clinically established drug-response biomarkers.
source: Applied to in vitro screening data on 265 compounds across 1074 cancer cell lines, our models identified 24 clinically established drug-response biomarkers
evidence: Direct statement of results from applying the GP model to the dataset

claim: The GP models provided evidence for six novel biomarkers by accounting for association with low uncertainty.

claim: The uncertainty estimates were validated with an additional drug screen of 26 drugs, 10 cell lines with 8 to 9 replicates.
source: We validated our uncertainty estimates with an additional drug screen of 26 drugs, 10 cell lines with 8 to 9 replicates.

claim: The two largest in vitro drug screening studies are GDSC and CTRP.
source: Currently the two largest in vitro drug screening studies, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) (Garnett et al., 2012; Iorio et al., 2016) and the Cancer Therapeutics Response Portal (CTRP) Rees et al., 2016
evidence: Direct statement with citations to the respective studies

claim: Some clinically-actionable biomarkers of drug response can be concordantly discovered between GDSC and CTRP.
source: Currently the two largest in vitro drug screening studies, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) (Garnett et al., 2012; Iorio et al., 2016) and the Cancer Therapeutics Response Portal (CTRP) Rees et al., 2016 have shown that some clinically-actionable biomarkers of drug response can be concordantly discovered (Iorio et al., 2016; Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Iorio et al., 2016 and Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015

claim: Different properties and mechanisms of drug response are best captured by different metrics dependent on the dose-response curve.
source: that different properties and mechanisms of drug response are best captured by different metrics dependent on the dose-response curve (Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2013

claim: Most HTS efforts focus on increasing throughput and often neglect experimental replicates.
source: Most HTS efforts focus on increasing throughput (Iorio et al., 2016; Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015) and thereby often neglect experimental replicates
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Iorio et al., 2016 and Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015

claim: Neglecting experimental replicates renders it impossible to correct for experimental noise, resulting in uncertainty for the estimated drug-response metrics.
source: Most HTS efforts focus on increasing throughput (Iorio et al., 2016; Seashore-Ludlow et al., 2015) and thereby often neglect experimental replicates, which renders it impossible to correct for experimental noise, resulting in uncertainty for the estimated drug-response metrics (e.g. IC50 value).
evidence: Logical inference from the lack of replicates

claim: Extrapolating IC50 values beyond the tested drug concentration range is particularly challenging and often unaccounted for in quality control metrics.
source: Extrapolating IC50 values beyond the tested drug concentration range is particularly challenging and often unaccounted for in quality control metrics (Haibe-Kains et al., 2013; Haverty et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haibe-Kains et al., 2013 and Haverty et al., 2016

claim: Most published studies using machine learning algorithms for predicting drug response assume that the measured drug responses are precise.
source: Most published studies using machine learning algorithms or mechanistic models for predicting drug response and biomarkers assume that the measured drug responses are precise (Costello et al., 2014; Keshava et al., 2019; Menden et al., 2019; Silverbush et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: If there is high uncertainty in measured drug-response values, the utility of machine learning methods for enhancing drug development may be severely limited.
source: If this assumption is not met and there is high uncertainty in the measured drug-response values, the utility of these methods for enhancing drug development may be severely limited (Costello et al., 2014; Menden et al., 2019; Silverbush et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costello et al., 2014, Menden et al., 2019, and Silverbush et al., 2017

claim: Most current models for curve fitting assume that cell viability has a sigmoidal relationship to the logarithm of the dose concentrations of the drug.
source: Most current models for curve fitting and describing dose-response data have primarily assumed that cell viability has a sigmoidal relationship to the logarithm of the dose concentrations of the drug (Dawson et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2010

claim: Gaussian Processes have been successfully used to measure uncertainty in noisy gene expression datasets.
source: Gaussian Processes (GP) are a flexible, probabilistic modelling technique that has been successfully used to measure uncertainty in noisy gene expression datasets (Lopez-Lopera and Alvarez, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lopez-Lopera and Alvarez, 2019

claim: Gaussian Processes have been incorporated into machine learning prediction of cell fates.
source: Gaussian Processes (GP) are a flexible, probabilistic modelling technique that has been successfully used to measure uncertainty in noisy gene expression datasets (Lopez-Lopera and Alvarez, 2019) and has been incorporated into machine learning prediction of cell fates (Boukouvalas et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boukouvalas et al., 2018

claim: Gaussian Processes cope well with regression tasks on dependent data and high dimensional covariates.

evidence: Supported by citations to Rasmussen and Williams, 2005 and Shi and Choi, 2011

source: First, for experiments where the estimated IC50 lies within the concentration range tested, the estimation uncertainty is positively correlated (Pearson correlation = 0.84, 95% CI [0.76, 0.89]) with the observation uncertainty.

claim: For experiments where the estimated IC50 lies beyond the maximum tested concentration, there is a negative correlation between estimation and observation uncertainty (Pearson correlation = −0.39, 95% CI [−0.51,–0.25]).

claim: Experiments with high estimation uncertainty from GPs were also the experiments with high Spearman correlation pointing to poor quality.
source: The experiments with high estimation uncertainty from our GPs were also the experiments with high Spearman correlation pointing to poor quality.

claim: IC50 values are highly concordant for sigmoid and GP-curve fittings, showing an average weighted Pearson correlation of 0.88 (95% CI [0.85; 0.91]) across individual drugs and cancer types.

claim: If >10% of cell lines responded within the concentration range, then a weighted Pearson correlation >0.75 was consistently achieved for all drugs.
